uncited: Adaptive sampling-based isosurface extraction constructs a mesh by sampling the implicit scalar field at discrete locations (typically octree leaves) rather than computing analytic intersections within grid cells.
This approach sacrifices geometric precision for computational efficiency and ease of implementation on adaptive structures.

It differs from its siblings by relying on discrete point clouds or simplified connectivity derived from samples, whereas methods like [Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree](2107-wilhelms-and-van-gelder-octree.md) or [Standard Interval Tree for Isosurface Extraction](1230-standard-interval-tree-for-isosurface-extraction.md) often preserve topological guarantees or analytic intersection logic within the spatial hierarchy.
The family shares the mechanism of using an octree to adaptively resolve the scalar field $V$.
The isosurface is defined by the set of sample points (usually octree leaves) where the field value crosses the isovalue $v$.

Unlike analytic methods that compute exact intersection coordinates on cell edges, these methods approximate the surface geometry using the sampled locations or simplified primitives associated with the leaves.
The primary challenge is maintaining topological consistency (avoiding cracks) and geometric accuracy when the sampling density varies across the surface.
Historical context: Early octree isosurfacing methods like [Wilhelms and Van Gelder Octree](2107-wilhelms-and-van-gelder-octree.md) established the foundation for adaptive spatial decomposition.

Later, [Ashida and Badla Octree Contouring](2117-ashida-and-badla-octree-contouring.md) and [Unconstrained Isosurface Extraction on Arbitrary Octrees](2413-unconstrained-isosurface-extraction-on-arbitrary-octrees.md) addressed topological issues.
In contrast, analytic methods (TetraSDF) achieved 4.56s and 0.28M vertices.
